title: Land Rover Series I–III
eyebrow: LAND ROVER · SERIES I, II, IIA, III · 1948–1985
verdict: A tractor that learned to do 55 mph, built from aluminium because steel was rationed, and still the vehicle that taught most of the world what a 4x4 is. Slow, loud, honest, and fixable with the tools in a farm shed.

paragraphs: The Series Land Rover is the original: a boxed steel ladder frame, two beam axles on leaf springs, a four-speed gearbox and flat aluminium panels you can unbolt with hand tools. It was meant to be a stopgap for a car company with an empty factory, and it outlived nearly everything else that company built. Today a good one is a collector's car with a Hagerty valuation, but underneath it is still a farm implement, and the owners who get the most out of them treat it exactly like one.

story.heading: A JEEP, A FARM AND A STEEL SHORTAGE
paragraphs: After the war Rover had a bombed Coventry factory, a shortage of steel and no affordable car to build. Chief designer Maurice Wilks, who used an army-surplus Jeep on his farm on Anglesey, proposed a light agricultural and utility vehicle with a power take-off. The first prototype used a Jeep chassis, a Rover P3 engine and gearbox, Birmabright alloy bodywork and a steering wheel in the middle, which earned it the nickname 'centre steer'. Early trucks were painted light green because surplus aircraft cockpit paint was available.

The production truck dropped the centre steering and every Jeep part, gained its own transfer box, and was launched at the Amsterdam Motor Show in 1948 on an 80-inch wheelbase with a 1.6-litre four of about 50 bhp. The freewheel four-wheel-drive system was replaced during 1950–51 by a simpler dog-clutch arrangement. A Tickford-bodied, wood-framed Station Wagon arrived in 1949 and flopped, with fewer than 700 sold. Land Rover learned the lesson fast: wheelbases grew to 86 and 107 inches in 1954, then 88 and 109 in 1956, and a 2.0-litre diesel followed in 1957.

story.heading: SERIES II AND IIA: THE SHAPE EVERYONE DRAWS
paragraphs: The 1958 Series II brought David Bache's wider 'barrel side' body and the 2.25-litre petrol four, though the first 1,500 or so short-wheelbase trucks kept the 2.0. The 109 Station Wagon could be had as a 12-seater, which in Britain counted as a bus and dodged purchase tax. The IIA of 1961 added a 2.25 diesel, and from 1967 long-wheelbase models could have a 2.6-litre six with servo brakes. Just 811 of those were NADA (North American Dollar Area) trucks, the only long-wheelbase models built for the US and Canada.

By February 1968 total production was just under 600,000, with more than 70% exported, and sales peaked in 1969–70 at over 60,000 a year. From February 1969 home-market trucks moved their headlamps out of the grille panel and into the wings, which is the quickest way to tell a late IIA from an early one. Hagerty notes that because so few were sold in the US, a IIA feels more exotic here than a comparable Jeep or [[land-cruiser/fj40|Land Cruiser]], and the market has priced that in.

story.heading: SERIES III AND THE LONG GOODBYE
paragraphs: The 1971 Series III was a modernisation by Land Rover standards: synchromesh on all four forward gears, a plastic grille, a moulded plastic dashboard with the instruments moved in front of the driver, and the 2.25's compression raised from 7:1 to 8:1. Long-wheelbase trucks got the one-piece Salisbury rear axle as standard. The millionth Land Rover rolled off the line in 1976, but North American factory sales had already ended in 1974, so most Series IIIs in the US arrived later through private import.

Land Rover kept fixing the known weak spots. In 1980 the 2.25 petrol and diesel engines got five-main-bearing crankshafts and the axles and hubs were strengthened, and in 1982 the driveshaft spline count went from 10 to 24 to deal with rear half-shafts that snapped under overloaded commercial use. A County station wagon trim arrived in April 1982, and a Stage 1 V8 (the Rover 3.5 detuned to 91 hp, with permanent four-wheel drive) ran from 1979 to 1985. Roughly 440,000 Series IIIs were built before the coil-sprung [[land-rover/defender-90-110|One Ten and Ninety]] took over.

story.heading: WHY THEY STILL MATTER
paragraphs: A Series truck is about as mechanically transparent as a motor vehicle gets. There is no ECU, the body panels unbolt, the rear half-shafts slide out of fully floating hubs without even jacking the truck up, and the parts catalogue from Vermont to Solihull is still enormous. The same simplicity explains its faults: leaf springs ride hard, the gearbox wears out first and second, the steel chassis and bulkhead rot where mud sits, and a 2.25 petrol is happiest at 50–55 mph.

None of that has hurt values. In 2019 Hagerty reported a median 'Excellent' value of $39,000 for Series II/IIA trucks, with petrol engines worth more than diesels and soft-tops slightly ahead of wagons. Every boxy 4x4 on this site, from the [[range-rover/classic|Range Rover Classic]] to the [[grenadier/station-wagon|Ineos Grenadier]], is in some way an argument with this vehicle about how much comfort a working truck is allowed to have.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE ODD ONES
callout.title: Lightweights, Forward Controls and Pink Panthers
paragraphs: The military took Series trucks in directions civilians never saw. The Lightweight was an air-portable military 88, and the Dutch and Danish versions ran diesel engines. The 109-based 'Pink Panther' Long-Range Desert Patrol Vehicles were converted by Marshall's of Cambridge for the SAS, with doors and windscreens removed, weapon mounts added and extra fuel and water tanks fitted.

Civilian oddballs exist too. The Series IIA Forward Control of 1962 put the cab over a 2.25 petrol engine, and the later 101 Forward Control used the 3.5 V8. The One Ton 109, built from late 1968 to 1977, combined a standard 109 body with a 2.6 six, a lower-ratio transfer box and 900x16 tyres. Only 170 IIA and 238 Series III One Tons were built for the home market.

engineering_intro: Every Series truck uses the same basic recipe: a fully boxed, welded steel ladder frame, beam axles on semi-elliptic leaf springs, a four-speed gearbox with a two-speed transfer box, and selectable four-wheel drive. The body is aluminium alloy panels bolted to the frame and a steel bulkhead, a choice made in 1948 because steel was rationed and kept even after aluminium became more expensive. The result is light, rust-resistant on top and rust-prone underneath, and almost entirely serviceable with hand tools.

engineering.note: Rear crossmember and outriggers are the usual rot spots.
Birmabright on the first trucks; corrodes where it touches steel.
Parabolic springs are the common comfort upgrade.
Freewheel system replaced around 1950; Stage 1 V8 got permanent 4WD.
Salisbury standard on Series III 109; some late IIAs had it too.
Full synchromesh only from the Series III.

buying_checks.head: Chassis rear crossmember and outriggers
buying_checks.body: These are repaired or replaced more than anything else on a Series frame. Feel along the top of the box sections and above the bump stops, where off-road loads concentrate. Heavy rot can mean a replacement chassis, which series123's guide puts at £1,000-plus in the UK, so make sure the price reflects it.

buying_checks.head: Bulkhead and door hinges
buying_checks.body: Check the lower bulkhead, the footwell corners and around the door hinges, plus anywhere the aluminium body touches steel: body-to-chassis mounts and where the wings bolt to the bulkhead. Serious bulkhead rot usually means the body has to come off.

buying_checks.head: Gearbox jumping out
buying_checks.body: First and second wear and can jump out of gear. Press and release the throttle in each gear on the test drive, try every ratio including low range, and listen for noises. The series123 guide rates the Series III gearbox as weaker than the Series II's.

buying_checks.head: Mismatched differentials
buying_checks.body: Owners sometimes fit a taller rear differential for economy. If front and rear ratios don't match, the truck will fight itself in four-wheel drive. Drive a short distance on soft ground to confirm 4WD engages and behaves.

buying_checks.head: Half-shafts and drive flanges
buying_checks.body: A clunk from the rear when you come to a stop (the 'Salisbury clunk' on later trucks) usually means worn splines in the drive flange. Rovers North forum members report flanges strip out occasionally and recommend carrying a spare. Check for play in the propshaft UJs too.

buying_checks.head: Springs and mounts
buying_checks.body: Leaves should be uniform and the truck should sit level. Look for cracked or welded spring hangers; rust at the spring mounts is an MOT failure in the UK.

buying_checks.head: Engine health
buying_checks.body: Low knocking points to worn crank bearings; a lighter, rapid tapping may just be tappets needing adjustment. Occasional blue smoke can be valve-stem seals, continuous blue smoke means rings and bores, and black smoke points at the carburettor.

buying_checks.head: Wheels and tyres
buying_checks.body: Original Series rims are tube-type. Tubeless radials need wheels with safety humps (later Defender-style wheels), and you shouldn't run tubes in tubeless wheels. Check what's fitted before you assume the tyres are a simple swap.

repairs.title: Swivel housing rebuild (Series IIA/III)
repairs.symptoms: Oil weeping past the swivel seal, pitted chrome on the swivel ball, wandering or heavy steering.
repairs.fix: Strip the hub and swivel housing, fit the new top pin, Railko bush with bottom wafer, bottom bearing and race, gaskets and swivel seal. Rovers North says to soak the Railko bush and wafer in 75-90 gear oil overnight and to lubricate the assembly with 75-90 oil rather than grease packs. Set preload with top-pin shims (removing shims tightens it), measuring turning effort with a spring scale with the big seal removed and the bolts fully tightened. Take the preload range from the workshop manual for your model.
repairs.tools: Spring/fish scale, torque wrench, hub nut spanner · Rovers North RNA3181P swivel rebuild kit (IIA 1962–71 and Series III non-V8, one side, no ball) · 75-90 gear oil

parts.name: RNA3181P swivel ball rebuild kit, Series IIA/III (one side)
DA3181P swivel housing repair kit (without housing), Series 2A–3
DA3181 swivel housing repair kit with housing, Series 2A–3

repairs.title: Rear half-shaft and drive flange swap
repairs.symptoms: Clunk when stopping or taking up drive, a wheel that won't drive, or a snapped shaft (usually at the diff end).
repairs.fix: The rear hubs are fully floating, so the shaft can come out without jacking the truck. Remove the six drive-flange bolts and the hub cap, pull the flange and shaft, and inspect the splines on both. Fit a new flange (and shaft if needed), clean both mating faces, add a thin film of RTV, and refit the six bolts to the specified torque. Upgraded 24-spline shafts are common; check flange bolt patterns (Series flanges have six bolts, Defender flanges five) before ordering.
repairs.tools: Sockets, torque wrench, RTV sealant · drive flange, half-shaft, gasket

repairs.title: Leaf spring and chassis bush replacement
repairs.time: A weekend for all four springs
repairs.symptoms: Clonks over bumps, the truck leaning or sitting low, cracked or perished bushes, or you're fitting parabolics.
repairs.fix: Take the springs and shackles off first, then deal with the chassis bushes. Rovers North members drive the old bush out with an air chisel and a worn socket the size of the outer shell, or burn the rubber out with a MAPP torch once the bolt is free, then cut the remaining shell lengthwise with a reciprocating saw from the inside out without cutting the frame. Fit new bushes and springs following the workshop manual.
repairs.tools: Air chisel or MAPP torch, reciprocating saw, drifts, jack and stands · spring and chassis bushes, shackle pins, springs (or parabolics)

parts.name: DA4106 parabolic springs, front pair, Series SWB & LWB
DA4107 parabolic springs, rear pair (3-leaf), Series

repairs.title: Clutch cross-shaft pins
repairs.time: A day with the floor out
repairs.cost: Pins and bushes are cheap; a seized pin can mean gearbox removal
repairs.symptoms: Clutch pedal suddenly stops a quarter to a third of the way down and the clutch won't disengage, while the hydraulics still work through their full stroke when disconnected.
repairs.fix: Disconnect the slave push rod and work the pedal to confirm the master and slave are fine. Lift the floor panels to reach the cross-shaft, check the pins, coupling tube and spherical bushes, then replace sheared pins (one Rovers North contributor recommends hardened pins), a coupling with elongated holes, and worn bushes. In one reported case a sheared pin was seized in the shaft and the transmission had to come out.
repairs.tools: Basic hand tools, drifts · clutch cross-shaft pins, coupling, cross-shaft bushes

repairs.title: Rear crossmember and outrigger repair
repairs.cost: Panels are cheap; welding is the bill
repairs.symptoms: Flaking or perforated steel at the rear crossmember, soft outriggers, fresh underseal hiding something.
repairs.fix: Clean back to bare metal and assess. Outriggers and rear crossmembers are bolt-on or weld-in replacement sections; cut out the rotten section, fit the new one square to the frame and seam-weld it, then protect the inside of the box sections. If the main rails are thin as well, a galvanised replacement chassis is the permanent answer.
repairs.tools: Welder, grinder, cutting discs, rust protection · replacement crossmember and outriggers or a galvanised chassis

repairs.title: Fit 235/85R16s and set the steering stops
repairs.symptoms: Tyres touching the frame at full lock after fitting larger or wider tyres.
repairs.fix: 235/85R16 is the most-recommended size on the Rovers North forum, close to (but a little wider than) the factory 7.50x16 option. If the tyres touch the chassis at full lock, wind out the steering stop bolts on the swivel housings until there's clearance. Expect a slightly bigger turning circle.
repairs.tools: Spanners · 235/85R16 tyres on suitable rims (tube-type Series rims need tubes; tubeless tyres want rims with safety humps)

repairs.title: Steering relay: free it, reseal it, refill it
repairs.time: A day; the radiator has to come out
repairs.cost: One owner's rebuild cost about $8; a replacement relay was about $100 plus shipping (Rovers North forum)
repairs.symptoms: Steering that is very heavy or tight, especially on a truck that has stood outside for years, or oil weeping from the bottom of the relay.
repairs.fix: The relay is the box-shaped unit in the chassis crossmember ahead of the radiator. It isn't the steering box at the foot of the column. Rule out dry ball joints and the steering damper first. Rovers North forum members say the radiator has to come out to reach the relay bracket bolts. A stubborn relay can be rebuilt without pulling it from the chassis, and one owner freed a seized unit with a 3 ft pipe over the arm. Inside, the bushes need lubrication. One owner found his 'bone dry' and could turn the shaft by hand with pliers after the rebuild. For a leak, members say you can remove the retaining ring and bottom plate and fit a new seal without stripping the whole relay. Refill with 90-weight gear oil.
repairs.tools: Spanners and sockets · ball-joint splitter · 3 ft pipe for leverage · relay seals · 90-weight gear oil

repairs.title: Gearbox jumping out of gear: find the cause
repairs.time: An hour for the external checks; a weekend or more if the gearbox comes out
repairs.cost: Detent springs and adjustments are cheap; internal repairs are parts plus a lot of labor
repairs.symptoms: The lever pops out of gear, often second or fourth, on the overrun or over bumps. Some owners resort to holding it in, or to a bungee cord on long trips.
repairs.fix: Start with the cheap checks that Rovers North forum members suggest. Look for play in the gear lever and its mounting: one owner tightened it and it 'totally' stopped jumping out of second. The same owner also found a dragging, bent clutch disc. Next, take off the top PTO cover and check the mainshaft nut for free play; an overdrive has to come off to reach it. With the cover off, inspect the selector forks and detent springs. Worn forks, a loose circlip on the gear cluster or worn synchros mean the box comes out. If the speedo also wanders and transfer-box oil leaks between the handbrake drum and its backing plate, one member says the rear output shaft nut has backed off. It gets 90 ft-lb.
repairs.tools: Spanners and sockets · torque wrench · top cover gasket · transmission jack if the box has to come out

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: 235/85R16 is the size most owners recommend: a Rovers North forum member calls it close to, but a little wider than, the factory-optional 7.50x16, and it should fit a stock 88 or 109 once the steering stops are adjusted so the tyre clears the frame at full lock (expect a slightly bigger turning circle). 215/85R16 is also close to 7.50x16. 265/75R16 on stock 5.5-inch rims rubbed the frame by about half to three-quarters of an inch for one owner, and another found 265s too wide on a 109. Original rims are tube-type, so check the wheels before fitting tubeless radials.

faq.q: What's the difference between a Series I, II, IIA and III?
faq.a: Series I (1948–58) has flat sides and 80, 86/88 or 107/109-inch wheelbases. Series II (1958–61) brought the wider 'barrel side' body and the 2.25 petrol. Series IIA (1961–71) looks almost identical but added the 2.25 diesel and the 2.6 six, and late home-market IIAs have headlamps in the wings. Series III (1971–85) has a plastic grille, a plastic dash with instruments in front of the driver and an all-synchro gearbox.

faq.q: Which years are the best to buy?
faq.a: Depends what you want. Series Is are the collectors' trucks. Classic Car Hub calls an 88- or 109-inch Series IIA the sweet spot, with good parts supply and a well-documented spec. Octane says the Series III is by far the easiest to live with and recommends a short-wheelbase 2.25 petrol for most buyers, or a Stage 1 V8 if you want something special; Series123 notes the III's gearbox isn't as strong as the II's. Heritage Parts Centre also rates the 2.25 petrol the preferable engine.
faq.src: CLASSIC CAR HUB · OCTANE · SERIES123 · HERITAGE PARTS CENTRE

faq.q: Were Series Land Rovers sold new in the US?
faq.a: Yes, but not many. Factory sales to North America ended in 1974. Only 811 of the long-wheelbase IIAs with the 2.6 six were NADA (North American Dollar Area) trucks, the only long-wheelbase models built for the US and Canada.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Owners on AULRO report roughly 14–17 mpg (imperial) for a 2.25 petrol in normal use, with a best of about 21 mpg at a steady 50 mph in a short-wheelbase truck. Loaded, hilly driving pulls it back toward 14. In US gallons, knock about a sixth off those figures.

Owners on the Rovers North forum put the comfortable cruise for a 2.25 petrol at 55–60 mph. With a Fairey overdrive, 60–65 on the flat is realistic. One owner advises 3,000–3,400 rpm for the four-cylinder petrol and warns that sitting at 4,000-plus wears engines out faster.

faq.q: Why do Series rear half-shafts break?
faq.a: Partly the design of the shafts and partly overloading in commercial use. Land Rover strengthened the axles and hubs in 1980 and increased the driveshaft spline count from 10 to 24 in 1982. Forum members say shafts usually break at the differential end, and worn drive flanges announce themselves with a clunk well before they strip.

faq.q: Should I fit free-wheeling front hubs?
faq.a: Rovers North advises against it on Series IIA/III swivels with the Railko bush: running the hubs unlocked stops the front driveline turning, which it says starves the swivel ball, Railko bush and front propshaft of lubrication. If you fit them anyway, lock them in regularly.

faq.q: Petrol or diesel? Soft top or wagon?
faq.a: On value, Hagerty found in 2019 that Series II/IIA petrol trucks were worth about 6% more than diesels and soft-tops about 2% more than wagons. In use, the 2.25 petrol is the more pleasant road engine; the early 2.0 and 2.25 diesels are slow even by Series standards.

The aluminium body doesn't rust but corrodes where it touches steel. The steel parts do rust: rear crossmember, outriggers, chassis box sections above the bump stops, the lower bulkhead and footwells, door hinge areas and door bottoms.

faq.q: Can I put tubeless tyres on the original wheels?
faq.a: Not properly. Original Series rims are tube-type. Tubeless radials need wheels with safety humps, which later Defender wheels have. Don't fit inner tubes in tubeless wheels.
Just under 600,000 by February 1968, more than 70% of them exported. The 1,000,000th Land Rover was built in 1976, and about 440,000 Series IIIs were made between 1971 and 1985.

mods.why: Seals, swivel kits, brakes, wiring and panels: the catalogues Series owners actually order from on both sides of the Atlantic.
Worn first and second gears and tired transfer boxes are the classic Series drivetrain complaints; rebuilt units and uprated parts exist.
When the rear crossmember, outriggers and rails have all been patched, a hot-dip galvanised frame ends the argument.
Canvas, seats and door tops wear out; LRO has a video on fitting an Exmoor Trim soft top to an ex-military Series III.
A Series has no crash structure to speak of; external and internal cages are the sensible addition for trail use. Series cages are built to order.

baseline_service.intro: A Series truck has no service computer and no idea when it was last looked after, so assume nothing: change every oil, grease every nipple and adjust every brake before you trust it. The Series Land Rover owner's 'green bible' (workshop manual) lists the full service schedule; the items below are what owners on LandyZone and Rovers North treat as the catch-up.

items.spec: 20W-50 mineral oil (the period handbook specified a 20W grade) · 2.25: about 1.9 US gal (≈7.2 L) including the filter (Series123); one owner's shop manual gives 13 pints plus 1.8 pints for the filter, which he works out as 7.4 US qt (≈7 L)
items.note: Owners stick with mineral oil; one warns that semi-synthetics can loosen old deposits in a worn engine. Petrol and diesel 2.25s use element-type or spin-on filters depending on year.

parts.name: RTC3184 oil filter element, 2.25 petrol & diesel

items.spec: Oil-bath canister on most trucks · refill grade [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.interval: Clean and refill at every oil change; more often in dust
items.note: If a previous owner swapped to an SU carburettor, check the SU dashpot has oil too.

items.spec: Points gap and timing per manual · plugs N12Y (8:1 CR) or N8 (7:1 CR)
items.interval: Check points and timing at every service
items.note: Owners list checking the points gap as a routine job; match the plug to your engine's compression ratio.

parts.name: RTC3570 spark plug N12Y, 2.25 petrol 8:1 CR

items.interval: Test at purchase; replace failed plugs
items.note: Hard cold starts on a 2.25 diesel usually mean heater plugs before anything more expensive.

items.spec: Antifreeze mix [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for type and capacity]
items.interval: Flush and refill now; then per manual
items.note: Check the block drain plug and core plugs for weeps while it's drained.

items.spec: EP90 gear oil · Series II/IIA: gearbox 2.5 imp pt (3 US pt, ≈1.4 L), transfer box 4.5 imp pt (≈5.5 US pt, ≈2.6 L), per Series123 and the workshop manual quoted on the Rovers North forum · Series III [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.interval: Drain and refill now; then per manual
items.note: Check the transfer box output seal: oil leaking past it soaks the transmission handbrake shoes. Owners buy EP90 in 20 L drums because a Series uses a lot of it.

items.spec: EP90 gear oil · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.interval: Drain and refill now; then per manual
items.note: Don't put one-shot swivel grease in the diffs; owners say drain it if someone has.

items.spec: 75-90 gear oil on IIA/III with the Railko bush (Rovers North)
items.interval: Check level every service; refill now
items.note: Rovers North advises oil, not grease packs, for the Railko bush, and warns that running free-wheeling hubs unlocked starves the swivels of lubrication.

items.spec: Grease all nipples: propshaft UJs and sliding joints, steering and spring shackles
items.note: 'Do all the grease nipples' is the first line of most owners' service lists.

parts.name: RTC3346HS 82 mm propshaft universal joint, Series

items.spec: Check play and adjust; check the front hubs are full
items.note: Wider tyres are harder on wheel bearings, according to Rovers North forum members.

parts.name: RTC3534 wheel bearing kit, Series 2/2A/3 to 1980

items.spec: Brake fluid [CONFIRM IN MANUAL for DOT grade] · adjust drum brakes
items.interval: Fluid every 2 years; adjust shoes at every service
items.note: Series drum brakes need regular manual adjustment; owners note they will need adjusting on any truck you buy.

parts.name: STC3945 front brake shoes (axle set), Series 2/2A/3 LWB six-cylinder & V8, 101 FC only

items.interval: Bleed or flush with the brakes
items.note: 'Don't forget the clutch' — the slave cylinder is easy to overlook.

parts.name: 8G8600L clutch slave cylinder repair kit, Series 1958–1984

items.note: Old tanks shed rust and sediment; a new filter is cheap insurance.
